source: IB Mathematics: applications and interpretation guide, first assessment 2021 (updated November 2020)

bullets.text: Do arithmetic with numbers in standard form a × 10^k, taking 1 ≤ a < 10 and k any integer.
Write standard form properly (5.2 × 10^30), never in calculator notation such as 5.2E30.
Recognise an arithmetic sequence and find its nth term from the first term and common difference.
Find the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence.
Write and evaluate arithmetic sums in sigma notation.
Apply arithmetic sequences to contexts such as simple interest, using technology (spreadsheet or GDC) to list terms and identify first term and difference.
Judge and predict from real data that is only roughly arithmetic, approximating the common difference.

booklet.label: The nth term of an arithmetic sequence
The sum of n terms of an arithmetic sequence

bullets.text: Recognise a geometric sequence and find its nth term from the first term and common ratio.
Find the sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence.
Write and evaluate geometric sums in sigma notation.
Apply geometric sequences to contexts such as disease spread, salary change and population growth, using technology and identifying first term and ratio.
Link geometric sequences to exponential models (topic 2) and regression (topic 4).

booklet.label: The nth term of a geometric sequence
The sum of n terms of a finite geometric sequence

bullets.text: Model compound interest with geometric sequences, compounding yearly, half-yearly, quarterly or monthly.
Model annual depreciation with geometric sequences.
Use technology, including built-in financial packages, for these problems; simple interest can lead in to compound interest.
Find the real value of an investment given an interest rate and an inflation rate.
Deriving the compound-interest formula is not examined.
Apply the laws of exponents to integer exponents (products, quotients, powers, negative exponents), e.g. 6^4 ÷ 6^3 = 6 and 2x^−3 = 2/x^3.
Know that a^x = b means log_a b = x (with b > 0), and that log_e x is ln x; introduce base-10 and base-e logarithms.
Evaluate logarithms numerically with technology.
Round to a given number of decimal places or significant figures, choosing an accuracy that suits the given data.
Find upper and lower bounds of rounded numbers, e.g. x = 4.1 to one decimal place means 4.05 ≤ x < 4.15.

Calculate percentage errors, including measurement errors from rounding or measurement limits, e.g. the maximum percentage error in a circle's area when the radius is measured as 2.5 cm to one decimal place.
Estimate, and recognise whether the results of calculations are reasonable, e.g. a length cannot be negative.
Solve amortization and annuity problems using technology, such as the built-in financial packages of a GDC or a spreadsheet.
In exams, payments are made at the end of each period.
Knowing the annuity formula helps understanding but is not examined.
Use technology to solve systems of linear equations in up to 3 variables.
Use technology to solve polynomial equations, using standard terms such as zeros and roots.
In exams no specific method of solution is required, and a system of equations always has a unique solution.
Use the laws of logarithms: log_a xy = log_a x + log_a y, log_a (x/y) = log_a x − log_a y and log_a x^m = m log_a x, for a, x, y > 0.
In exams the base a is 10 or e.
Simplify numerical and algebraic expressions with rational exponents, e.g. 5^(1/2) × 5^(1/3) = 5^(5/6), 6^(3/4) ÷ 6^(1/2) = 6^(1/4), 32^(3/5) = 8 and x^(−1/2) = 1/√x.
Find the sum of an infinite geometric sequence.
Link to limits (SL 5.1), fractals (AHL 3.9) and Markov chains (AHL 4.19).

booklet.label: The sum of an infinite geometric sequence

bullets.text: Know the number i, where i^2 = −1.
Write complex numbers in Cartesian form z = a + bi, and use the terms real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument.
Calculate sums, differences, products and quotients by hand and with technology, and powers of complex numbers in Cartesian form with technology.
Use the complex plane, using and drawing Argand diagrams.
Find complex solutions of quadratic equations ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0, real coefficients) where b^2 − 4ac < 0, linking the quadratic formula to the graph of f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c.

items.name: Complex numbers in polar and exponential form

bullets.text: Write a complex number in modulus–argument (polar) form z = r(cosθ + i sinθ) = r cisθ.
Write a complex number in exponential (Euler) form z = re^(iθ).
Convert between Cartesian, polar and exponential forms, by hand and with technology.
Calculate products, quotients and integer powers in polar or exponential form.
Finding the roots of complex numbers is not examined.
Add sinusoidal functions with the same frequency but different phase shift angles, e.g. combine AC voltages V1 = 10cos(40t) and V2 = 20cos(40t + 10) into V = A cos(40t + B).
Interpret complex numbers geometrically: addition and subtraction as vector addition and subtraction, and multiplication as a rotation and a stretch in the Argand diagram.
Define a matrix and use the terms element, row, column and order for m × n matrices.
Use matrix algebra for m × n matrices: equality, addition, subtraction and multiplication by a scalar, including with technology.
Multiply matrices, including to solve practical problems.
Know that matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but not commutative.
Use the identity matrix I and the zero matrix 0.
Find determinants and inverses of n × n matrices with technology, and of 2 × 2 matrices by hand.
Know that a system of linear equations can be written as Ax = b.
Solve systems of equations using the inverse matrix; in exams A is always invertible, except when solving for eigenvectors.
Model and solve real-life problems such as coding and decoding messages and solving systems of equations.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Find the characteristic polynomial of a 2 × 2 matrix.
Diagonalize a 2 × 2 matrix, restricted to the case where there are distinct real eigenvalues.

Apply this to powers of 2 × 2 matrices with M^n = PD^nP^(−1), where P is a matrix of eigenvectors and D a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, e.g. movement of population between two towns or predator–prey models.
Calculations by hand and with technology are only expected for 2 × 2 matrices.
Write and convert between gradient-intercept, general and point-gradient forms of a line.
Find the gradient and intercepts of a line.
Use m1 = m2 for parallel lines and m1 × m2 = −1 for perpendicular lines.
Calculate gradients in real settings such as roads and bridges.
Explain function, domain, range and graph, and use notation such as f(x), v(t), C(n); e.g. f(x) = √(2 − x) has domain x ≤ 2 and range f(x) ≥ 0.
Treat a function as a mathematical model; a graph helps to see the range.
Understand an inverse as undoing the function, as a reflection in y = x, written f^−1(x).
Solve f(x) = 10 as finding f^−1(10); inverses exist for one-to-one functions, and the domain of f^−1 is the range of f.
Know the graph of y = f(x) from its equation.
Sketch a graph from given information or a context, including moving a graph from screen to paper.
Use technology to graph functions, including sums and differences of functions.
Distinguish draw from sketch, and label axes and key features; graphs may include functions not named in topic 2.
Read key features off graphs with technology: extremes, intercepts, symmetry, vertex, zeros, and vertical or horizontal asymptotes.
Find intersection points of two curves or lines with technology.

items.name: Modelling with functions
items.practice: Modelling with quadratic and cubic functions
alsoPractises: Modelling with linear and piecewise functions

bullets.text: Model with linear functions f(x) = mx + c, including piecewise linear models such as the depth of a swimming pool or mobile phone charges.
Model with quadratic functions f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c (a ≠ 0): axis of symmetry, vertex, zeros and roots, and intercepts on the x- and y-axes; technology can be used to find roots.
Model exponential growth and decay with f(x) = ka^x + c, f(x) = ka^(−x) + c (a > 0) and f(x) = ke^(rx) + c, and find the equation of the horizontal asymptote.
Model direct and inverse variation with f(x) = ax^n, n ∈ ℤ, where the y-axis is a vertical asymptote when n < 0.
Model with cubic functions f(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d.
Model with sinusoidal functions f(x) = a sin(bx) + d and f(x) = a cos(bx) + d.
For sinusoidal models you only predict or find the amplitude |a|, the period 360°/b and the principal axis y = d; translating between sin x and cos x is not expected.

booklet.label: Axis of symmetry of the graph of a quadratic function

bullets.text: Use the modelling process to create, fit and use the models of SL 2.5 and their graphs.
Develop and fit a model: given a context, recognise and choose an appropriate model and possible parameters.
Determine a reasonable domain for a model.
Find the parameters of a model by solving equations simultaneously with technology, from initial conditions, or by substituting points into a given function.
Test and reflect: comment on whether a model is appropriate and reasonable.
Justify the choice of a model from the shape of the data, the properties of the curve and/or the context.
Use the model: read, interpret and make predictions from it, aware of the dangers of extrapolation.
At SL non-linear regression is not expected (regression is in topic 4), but you set up and solve up to three linear equations in three variables with technology.
Use composite functions in context.
Use the notation (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)), with (f ∘ f^−1)(x) = (f^−1 ∘ f)(x) = x.
Use the inverse function f^−1, including domain restriction, e.g. f(x) = (x − 3)^2 − 2 has an inverse if the domain is restricted to x ≥ 3 or to x ≤ 3.
Find an inverse function.
Transform the graphs of all functions in topic 2 (SL and AHL), and others met when modelling real-life situations.
Apply translations y = f(x) + b and y = f(x − a); a translation by the vector (3, −2) moves the graph 3 units right and 2 units down.
Apply reflections in the x-axis, y = −f(x), and in the y-axis, y = f(−x).
Apply a vertical stretch with scale factor p, y = pf(x), and a horizontal stretch with scale factor 1/q, y = f(qx); the x- and y-axes are invariant.

Combine transformations, where order matters, e.g. y = x^2 to y = 3x^2 + 2 by a vertical stretch of scale factor 3 then a translation by (0, 2), or y = sin x to y = 4sin2x by a vertical stretch of scale factor 4 and a horizontal stretch of scale factor 1/2.
Beyond the SL models, use exponential models to calculate half-life.
Model with natural logarithmic functions f(x) = a + b ln x.

Model with sinusoidal functions f(x) = a sin(b(x − c)) + d; radians are assumed unless degrees are shown (e.g. f(x) = sin x°), the period in radians is 2π/b, and a horizontal translation c is called a phase shift.

Model with logistic functions f(x) = L/(1 + Ce^(−kx)), L, C, k > 0, where growth is restricted (e.g. population on an island, bacteria in a petri dish, height of a person or seedling); the horizontal asymptote f(x) = L is the carrying capacity.

Model with piecewise functions, finding parameters that make the function continuous, e.g. a so that f(x) = 1 + x for 0 ≤ x < 2 and f(x) = ax^2 + x for x ≥ 2 is continuous; the formal definition of continuity is not required.
Interpret and use other models introduced in an exam question.
Scale very large or very small numbers using logarithms, choosing a manageable scale when data have a wide range or when the rate of growth matters more than the absolute value.
Linearize data with logarithms to decide whether it has an exponential or a power relationship, using best-fit straight lines to find the parameters.
Interpret log-log and semi-log graphs; you will not be asked to draw or sketch them in exams.

items.name: 3D distance, midpoint and measurement
items.practice: Volume and surface area of 3D shapes

bullets.text: Find the distance between two points in 3D and their midpoint.
Find volume and surface area of right pyramids, right cones, spheres, hemispheres and combinations of these solids.
Measure the angle where two lines meet, or the angle a line makes with a plane.
At SL, only right-angled trigonometry is set in 3D; identify right-angled triangles inside solids to find lengths and angles.

booklet.label: Distance between two points (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2)
Coordinates of the midpoint of a line segment with endpoints (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2)
Area of the curved surface of a cone

bullets.text: Use sine, cosine and tangent to find sides and angles of right-angled triangles.
Use the sine rule a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC.
Use the cosine rule c^2 = a^2 + b^2 − 2ab cosC and cosC = (a^2 + b^2 − c^2)/(2ab).
Find a triangle's area as ½ab sinC.
Draw well-labelled diagrams; use inverse functions for angles (SL 2.2); the ambiguous case of the sine rule is not included here.
Solve applied problems with right-angled and non-right-angled trigonometry plus Pythagoras's theorem; contexts may involve bearings.
Use angles of elevation and depression.
Draw labelled diagrams from a written description.
Find the length of an arc and the area of a sector of a circle.
Radians are not required at SL.
Find the equation of a perpendicular bisector, given either two points or the equation of a line segment and its midpoint.
Use the terms of Voronoi diagrams: sites, vertices, edges and cells.
Add a site to an existing Voronoi diagram.
Use nearest neighbour interpolation: every point in a cell can be estimated to have the same value (e.g. rainfall) as its site.
Apply Voronoi diagrams to the 'toxic waste dump' problem; in exams the solution point is always at an intersection of three edges.

In exams, site coordinates are given for calculating perpendicular bisector equations and you will not construct bisectors; questions may ask for the equation of a boundary, the site closest to a given point, or the area of a region.

items.name: Radians, arc length and sector area

bullets.text: Define a radian and convert between degrees and radians.
Use radians to find the area of a sector and the length of an arc, with radian measure as exact multiples of π or decimals.
Define cosθ and sinθ using the unit circle, and see how the graphs of sin x and cos x are built from it.
Use the Pythagorean identity cos^2θ + sin^2θ = 1.
Define tanθ as sinθ/cosθ.
Extend the sine rule to the ambiguous case.
Solve trigonometric equations in a finite interval using graphical methods.
Exact values of cosθ, sinθ and tanθ are not examined.
Transform points in two dimensions with matrices of the form (a b; c d)(x; y) + (e; f): reflections, horizontal and vertical stretches, enlargements, translations and rotations.
Compose these transformations, including iterative techniques to generate fractals.
Interpret the determinant of a transformation matrix geometrically: area of image = |det A| × area of object.

booklet.label: Transformation matrices: reflection in y = (tan θ)x

bullets.text: Know the concepts of a vector and a scalar.
Represent vectors as directed line segments.
Use unit vectors and the base vectors i, j, k.

Write a vector in components and as a column, v = (v1, v2, v3) = v1 i + v2 j + v3 k; add and subtract vectors, multiply by a scalar kv (parallel vectors) and find the magnitude |v| from components, algebraically and geometrically, including the resultant of two or more vectors.
Use the zero vector 0 and the vector −v.
Use position vectors OA→ = a.
Rescale and normalize vectors, with v/|v| the unit vector, e.g. find the velocity of a particle with speed 7 m s^−1 in the direction 3i + 4j.
Write the vector equation of a line in two and three dimensions, r = a + λb, where b is a direction vector of the line.
Convert to parametric form x = x0 + λl, y = y0 + λm, z = z0 + λn.

booklet.label: Parametric form of the equation of a line

bullets.text: Apply vectors to kinematics.

Model linear motion with constant velocity in two and three dimensions with r = r0 + vt: find positions, intersections, paths, times, and the time and distance when two objects are closest to each other; the relative position of B from A is AB→.
Model motion with variable velocity in two dimensions, e.g. (vx, vy) = (7, 6 − 4t); projectile and circular motion are special cases, and f(t − a) indicates a time shift of a.
Define and calculate the scalar product of two vectors.
Find the angle between two vectors using v · w = |v||w|cosθ, and the acute angle between two lines; v · w = 0 means the non-zero vectors are perpendicular.
Define and calculate the vector product v × w = |v||w|sinθ n, where n is the unit normal vector given by the right-hand screw rule.
Generalized properties and proofs of the scalar and vector products are not required.
Interpret |v × w| geometrically, using it for the area of a parallelogram (and hence a triangle).
Find components of vectors: the component of a in the direction of b is (a · b)/|b| = |a|cosθ, and the component of a perpendicular to b, in the plane of the two vectors, is |a × b|/|b| = |a|sinθ.
Use the terms graph, vertex, edge, adjacent vertices, adjacent edges and degree of a vertex, and represent real-world structures (circuits, maps) as weighted or unweighted graphs.
Recognise simple, complete and weighted graphs, and know the terms connected and strongly connected.
Use directed graphs, with the in-degree and out-degree of a vertex.
Identify subgraphs and trees.
Write and use adjacency matrices.
Understand walks.
Find the number of walks of length k (or less than k) between two vertices: the (i, j)th entry of A^k gives the number of k-length walks from i to j.
Use weighted adjacency tables, where weights could be costs, distances or lengths of time.
Construct the transition matrix for a strongly connected, undirected or directed graph, e.g. simple graphs as in the Google PageRank algorithm.

items.name: Spanning trees, postman and salesman problems

bullets.text: Use tree and cycle algorithms with undirected graphs.
Use the terms walk, trail, path, circuit and cycle.
Determine whether an Eulerian trail or circuit exists.
Find Hamiltonian paths and cycles.
Find minimum spanning trees with Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms, including the matrix method for Prim's.

Solve the Chinese postman problem to find the shortest route around a weighted graph with up to four odd vertices, going along each edge at least once; explain why the algorithm works, apply it and justify your choice of algorithm.

Use the travelling salesman problem to find the Hamiltonian cycle of least weight in a weighted complete graph, converting practical problems to the classical problem by completing a table of least distances where needed.
Find an upper bound for the travelling salesman problem with the nearest neighbour algorithm.
Find a lower bound for the travelling salesman problem with the deleted vertex algorithm.
Use the terms population, sample, random sample, discrete data and continuous data.
Judge how reliable a data source is and where sampling bias arises, including missing data and recording errors.
Interpret outliers: a value more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the nearest quartile; some are valid sample members, some are errors.
Know sampling techniques and their effectiveness: simple random, convenience, systematic, quota, stratified.
Present discrete and continuous data in frequency tables (class intervals as inequalities without gaps).
Draw histograms: frequency histograms with equal class intervals; frequency density histograms are not required.
Use cumulative frequency graphs to find median, quartiles, percentiles, range and IQR.
Draw and read box and whisker diagrams, with outliers marked by crosses; compare two distributions and judge from symmetry whether data may be normal.
Find mean, median and mode; find the mean both by formula and with technology.
Estimate the mean of grouped data from mid-interval values; find the modal class (equal class intervals only).
Find IQR, standard deviation and variance; standard deviation and variance of a data set use technology only, and squaring the standard deviation gives the variance.
Say how adding to or scaling all data values changes mean and standard deviation (e.g. subtract 3, or double all values).
Find quartiles of discrete data using technology, knowing that methods differ so by-hand and technology values may differ.

booklet.label: Mean, x̄, of a set of data

bullets.text: Describe linear correlation of bivariate data: positive, zero, negative; strong, weak, none.
Find Pearson's r with technology (hand calculation optional); critical values are given; r is only meaningful for linear relationships.
Draw scatter diagrams and lines of best fit by eye through the mean point.
Separate correlation from causation: correlation does not imply causation.
Find the regression line of y on x with technology, and use it for prediction.
Interpret the parameters a and b in y = ax + b.
Know the dangers of extrapolation, and that a y on x line cannot reliably predict x from y.
Use the vocabulary of probability: trial, outcome, equally likely, relative frequency, sample space (U), event; list sample spaces or tabulate them.
Find P(A) = n(A)/n(U), and tell experimental (relative frequency) from theoretical probability.
Use complementary events A and A′.
Find the expected number of occurrences, e.g. 128 students, P(absent) = 0.1, expect 12.8.
Find probabilities from Venn, tree and sample-space diagrams or outcome tables, with or without replacement.
Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), including the non-exclusive meaning of 'or'.
Use mutually exclusive events: P(A ∩ B) = 0.
Use conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A|B).
Use independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
Problems can be solved from diagrams without explicit formulae.

items.name: Discrete random variables and expected value

bullets.text: Work with discrete random variables and probability distributions given as a table or a formula such as P(X = x) = (1/18)(4 + x) for x in {1, 2, 3}.
Find the expected value E(X) of a discrete random variable.
Apply to problems; E(X) = 0 means a fair game where X is a player's gain.

booklet.label: Expected value of a discrete random variable X

bullets.text: Recognise situations modelled by a binomial distribution and find binomial probabilities with technology.
Use the mean and variance of a binomial distribution; the formal proof is not required.
Link to expected number of occurrences (SL 4.5).

booklet.label: Binomial distribution X ~ B(n, p): Mean
Binomial distribution X ~ B(n, p): Variance

bullets.text: Know the normal distribution and curve, its properties and diagrams, and its natural occurrence.
Know about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of data within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
Find normal probabilities with technology.
Find inverse normal values with technology when mean and standard deviation are given; no standardising to z is involved.
Find Spearman's rank correlation coefficient r_s using technology, averaging the ranks of equal data items.

Know when Pearson's and Spearman's coefficients are appropriate and their limitations: Pearson's tests only for linearity, Spearman's for any monotonic relationship, and Spearman's is less sensitive to outliers.
Derivation or proof of either coefficient is not required.
Formulate null and alternative hypotheses H0 and H1, as an equation, an inequality or in words.
Use significance levels.
Use p-values.
Find expected and observed frequencies.
Carry out the χ^2 test for independence using contingency tables, degrees of freedom and a critical value.
Carry out the χ^2 goodness of fit test.

In χ^2 exam questions: at most 4 rows or columns, degrees of freedom greater than one (n − 1 for goodness of fit at SL), critical values given where appropriate, the p-value and χ^2 statistic found with technology, upper-tail tests only at 1%, 5% or 10%, and expected frequencies greater than 5; compare the p-value with the significance level or the χ^2 statistic with the critical value.
Carry out the t-test, with calculations made using technology.

Use the p-value to compare the means of two populations: at SL samples are unpaired, population variance is unknown and assumed equal (pooled two-sample t-test), and the variables must be normally distributed; interpret the result of the test.
Use one-tailed and two-tailed tests.
Design valid data collection methods such as surveys and questionnaires, knowing biased and unbiased, personal, unstructured and structured (consistent answer choices), and precise questioning.
Select relevant variables from many variables.
Choose relevant and appropriate data to analyse.
Categorize numerical data in a χ^2 table and justify the categories, choosing them so that expected frequencies are greater than 5.
Choose an appropriate number of degrees of freedom when parameters are estimated from the data in a χ^2 goodness of fit test.
Define reliability and validity and know the difference.
Use reliability tests: test-retest and parallel forms.
Use validity tests: content and criterion-related.
Use regression with non-linear functions.
Evaluate least squares regression curves using technology; exam questions may use linear, quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and sine functions.
Use the sum of square residuals SS_res as a measure of fit for a model.
Use the coefficient of determination R^2, the proportion of variability in the second variable accounted for by the model, and know its connection to Pearson's r for linear models.
Evaluate R^2 using technology, aware that many factors affect a model's validity and R^2 alone is not a good way to decide between models.
Knowing R^2 = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot (so R^2 = 1 when SS_res = 0) helps understanding but is not examined.
Apply a linear transformation to a single random variable: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X); the variance formula itself is not required in exams.
Find the expected value of a linear combination of n random variables.
Find the variance of a linear combination of n independent random variables.
Use x̄ = Σ x_i/n as an unbiased estimate of μ.
Use s_(n−1)^2 = (n/(n − 1)) s_n^2 = Σ f_i(x_i − x̄)^2/(n − 1), where n = Σ f_i, as an unbiased estimate of σ^2.
Showing that E(X̄) = μ and E(s_(n−1)^2) = σ^2 is not examined.

booklet.label: Linear transformation of a single random variable: expectation
Linear transformation of a single random variable: variance
Linear combinations of n independent random variables: expectation
Linear combinations of n independent random variables: variance
Sample statistics: unbiased estimate of population variance

items.name: Sample mean and the central limit theorem
items.practice: Unbiased estimates and sample mean distribution

bullets.text: Know that a linear combination of n independent normal random variables is normally distributed; in particular X ~ N(μ, σ^2) ⇒ X̄ ~ N(μ, σ^2/n).
Use the central limit theorem: X̄ approaches normality for large n, how large depending on the distribution sampled; in exams n > 30 is sufficient.

booklet.label: Linear combinations of n independent random variables: expectation
Linear combinations of n independent random variables: variance

bullets.text: Find confidence intervals for the mean of a normal population, using the normal distribution when σ is known and the t-distribution when σ is unknown, regardless of sample size.
Interpret the results in context.
Use the Poisson distribution and its mean and variance, as a model when events are independent and occur at a uniform average rate.
Use the fact that the sum of two independent Poisson distributions has a Poisson distribution.
Choose between the normal, binomial and Poisson distributions for a given context.
Formal proofs of means and variances are not required.

items.name: Further hypothesis tests and errors
alsoPractises: Type I and Type II errors

bullets.text: Find critical values and critical regions; critical regions for t-tests are not required.

Test for a population mean of a normal distribution, using the normal distribution when σ is known and the t-distribution when σ is unknown, regardless of sample size; treat matched pairs as a single-sample technique.
Test for a proportion using the binomial distribution.
Test for a population mean using the Poisson distribution; Poisson and binomial tests are one-tailed only.
Use technology to test the hypothesis that the population product moment correlation coefficient ρ is 0 for bivariate normal distributions; in exams the data will be given.
Find Type I and Type II errors and calculate their probabilities, for normal (known variance), Poisson and binomial distributions.

For discrete random variables, tests and critical regions are one-tailed only, and the critical region maximizes the probability of a Type I error while keeping it less than the stated significance level.
Use transition matrices, with T_ij the probability of moving from state j to state i, and transition diagrams for discrete dynamical systems.
Find powers of transition matrices.
Use regular Markov chains.
Use initial state probability matrices: after n transitions the column state matrix is s_n = T^n s_0.
Find steady state and long-term probabilities by repeated multiplication of the transition matrix or by solving a system of linear equations; exam questions say when exact solutions are required.
Know that the steady state is the eigenvector for eigenvalue 1, with entries scaled to sum to 1.

items.name: Limits and derivative as rate of change

bullets.text: Meet the idea of a limit, estimating limit values from a table or graph; formal analytic methods of finding limits are not required.
Treat the derivative both as the slope function and as a rate of change; write it as dy/dx, f′(x), dV/dr or ds/dt.
Understand the gradient of a curve informally as a limit.
Identify increasing and decreasing functions and the intervals where they occur.
Interpret f′(x) > 0, f′(x) = 0 and f′(x) < 0 graphically.
Differentiate f(x) = ax^n to get anx^(n−1), for n an integer.
Differentiate sums of such terms, e.g. ax^n + bx^(n−1) + …, where all exponents are integers.
Get the equation of the tangent and of the normal at a chosen point, analytically and with technology.
Integrate ax^n + bx^(n−1) + … as anti-differentiation, for integer n ≠ −1.
Use a boundary condition to find the constant, e.g. dy/dx = 3x^2 + x with y = 10 at x = 1.
Evaluate definite integrals with technology.
Find the area between a curve y = f(x) > 0 and the x-axis; link anti-derivatives, definite integrals and area, and write a correct integral expression first.
Find the values of x where the gradient of a curve is zero.
Solve f′(x) = 0, using technology to generate f′(x) from f(x) and to find the solutions.
Find local maximum and minimum points, aware that a local maximum or minimum is not necessarily the greatest or least value of the function in the given domain.
Solve optimisation problems in context, e.g. maximizing profit, minimizing cost, maximizing volume for a given surface area.
Kinematics questions are not set in SL exams.
Estimate an area with the trapezoidal rule, from a table of data or a function, using intervals of equal width.
Link to upper and lower bounds (SL 1.6) and areas under curves (SL 5.5).
Differentiate sin x, cos x, tan x, e^x, ln x and x^n where n ∈ ℚ.
Use the chain rule, product rule and quotient rule.
Solve related rates of change problems.
Link to maximum and minimum points (SL 5.6) and optimisation (SL 5.7).
Find the second derivative, using the notation d^2y/dx^2 and f″(x).
Use the second derivative test to distinguish between a maximum and a minimum point.
Know that a point of inflexion is where the concavity changes, interpret it in context, and use concave-up for f″(x) > 0 and concave-down for f″(x) < 0.
Find definite and indefinite integrals of x^n where n ∈ ℚ (including n = −1), sin x, cos x, 1/cos^2 x and e^x.
Integrate by inspection, or by substitution of the form ∫ f(g(x))g′(x) dx, e.g. ∫ sin(2x + 5) dx, ∫ 1/(3x + 2) dx, ∫ 4x sin x^2 dx, ∫ sin x/cos x dx.
Find the area of the region enclosed by a curve and the x- or y-axis in a given interval, including negative integrals.
Find volumes of revolution about the x-axis or y-axis, V = ∫ πy^2 dx or V = ∫ πx^2 dy from a to b.

bullets.text: Solve kinematic problems involving displacement s, velocity v and acceleration a, with v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d^2s/dt^2 = v dv/ds.
Find displacement from t1 to t2 as ∫ v(t) dt and total distance travelled as ∫ |v(t)| dt.
Know that speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Use the notation ẋ = dx/dt and ẍ = d^2x/dt^2.

items.name: Setting up and separating differential equations

bullets.text: Set up a model or differential equation from a context, e.g. the growth of algae G at time t is proportional to √G.
Solve by separation of variables, e.g. an exponential model as the solution of dy/dx = ky, using the term 'general solution'.
Use and interpret slope fields and their diagrams.
Use Euler's method to find approximate solutions to first-order differential equations, using spreadsheets; in exams the values are generated using permissible technology.
Solve dy/dx = f(x, y) numerically.
Solve the coupled system dx/dt = f1(x, y, t) and dy/dt = f2(x, y, t) numerically, e.g. in predator–prey models.
Draw phase portraits for the solutions of coupled differential equations dx/dt = ax + by and dy/dt = cx + dy; systems have distinct, non-zero eigenvalues.

Analyse future paths qualitatively for distinct real, complex and imaginary eigenvalues: positive (or complex with positive real part) means all solutions move away from the origin; negative (or complex with negative real part) means they move towards it; complex gives a spiral; imaginary gives a circle or ellipse; real with different signs makes the origin a saddle point.
Sketch trajectories and use phase portraits to identify key features such as equilibrium points, stable populations and saddle points.
Exact solutions are only required for real distinct eigenvalues.

booklet.label: Exact solution for coupled linear differential equations

bullets.text: Solve d^2x/dt^2 = f(x, dx/dt, t) by Euler's method, writing it as the coupled first-order equations dx/dt = y and dy/dt = f(x, y, t).
Find exact solutions as in AHL 5.17; solutions of d^2x/dt^2 + a dx/dt + bx = 0 can also be investigated with the phase portrait method.
In exams the differential equation will be given.
